utterances.text: Yes, this was the forward command post and it became the main command post throughout this operation, which means that the report from the command of Zenica were sent to the forward command post of Luke, where then these reports were processed as daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us dwell on this document a while longer. Do you agree that this document tells about reporting of the subordinated units? Please take a look at what is stated below the delivered -- the phrase "delivered to," or "sent to."

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see. And not for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree that this document serves to inform that the reporting of commanders of the subordinate units to the commander of the 3rd Corps will be -- will take part at a certain date at a certain time and who is going to be attending that briefing?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can be seen and it is standard procedure to determine who should come where.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that El Mujahedin is not part of the briefing?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: El Mujahidin's representatives did not take part or attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they were not meant to attend?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not meant to attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we admit this document into evidence and can it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. And may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 388.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a clarification for the transcript. Page 45, line 23, my question concludes with the words "the El Mujahedin detachment" and then the witness said - it was his answer - [In English] "there is no marking and no mention." That was the witness's answer; whereas, the transcript shows as if it was all part of my question. I am doing my utmost not to speak too quickly today. Perhaps we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Would the counsel and the witness mind to pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the witness the following: In the plan that was studied by the staff, be it by General Delic or General Hadzihasanovic, there was no mention of the El Mujahedin detachment. Can you repeat your -- what your answer was.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no mention. It was not marked anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this should clear the mistake in the transcript. Has the latest document been given an exhibit number? It has. Thank you very much. Perhaps we can show D391 to the witness. For the record, it is an order of the 3rd Corps at Luke, which has to do with the team for direct command and control of the attack Operation Farz.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the document. Its first page, then the second page briefly. I presume you're familiar with the document. Do you agree with me that it is a 3rd Corps document signed by the commander?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does come from the 3rd Corps. It is the organisation of monitoring and control of the Farz operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore you agree with me that a team was put in place to directly control and plan this action.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is on the formation of a team which is supposed to immediately control the operation that had been planned from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this order was implemented?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was implemented in full, as stated in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps we could assign an exhibit number to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps to gain some time I would like to deal with the following topic briefly only.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the way of reporting between units was standard procedure? It was well-regulated. Namely, it was well-known which level of command can report to what level that comes next.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clearly stated who was to inform the General Staff, the corps command, and the subordinate units, including brigade commands. It was all regulated by separate orders, and those orders are usually entitled "The organisation of reporting in the units."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have a look at D393 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As we go to D393, Madam Vidovic, how much time do you still need? You've exhausted the 1 hour, 59 minutes that was used by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much, Your Honour. Twenty minutes at the most, depending on the answers. Maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D393. For the record, it is a document of the forward command post at Luke dated the 29th of August, 1995, ordering regular daily combat reporting of the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the document. Since we are -- do not have much time, can you confirm us -- to us that this is a 3rd Corps document?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an authentic document, and it was issued immediately prior to the combat activities regulating the way of reporting to the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 5, please. But before that, have a look at item 3. Do you agree that this order states that: "The reports will be sent by all subordinated commands and units in direct communication with the corps commander, except the units that are currently resubordinated to other units"?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In principle, it always had to be defined so as to avoid any confusion in the process of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Related to this, I wanted to ask you a simple question: Even had the El Mujahedin sent reports, according to this order, theoretically, hypothetically speaking, according this order, such orders would not have been sent to the 3rd Corps. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not supposed to, and they did not send any reports to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just get something clear here. This paragraph 3 however does say "except the units that are currently subordinated to other units." Is it -- am I correct to say that it is your evidence that the El Mujahedin detachment had been resubordinated to the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So by this very order, they were not expected to give their report, because they are accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, to clarify something, His Honour asked you the following: Judge Moloto asked you, which reads "it wasn't expected of them to send reports because they were accepted"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excepted, not accepted. Excepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excepted. Sorry. I apologise, Your Honour. Very well. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But so can you explain briefly why they were not expected [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the El Mujahedin was resubordinate to the 35th Division. It was not the resubordinated unit. I cannot tell you exactly which units there were subordinated to that division, though. I think it was the 3rd and the 4th Manoeuvre Detachment. However, this order stipulates that all the units should forward their reports apart from those that were resubordinated, who were lent, so to say, to another command. And I hope that is the way you understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. That's the explanation you gave me. You've just given it a second time and I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I want to move to a topic that you were not examined on still or yet, which has to do with the treatment of prisoners of war. Can we show Exhibit 385 to the witness, please. 384. That was a directive. Page 8. 384.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's exhibit, not document? Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as I said, exhibit. This is the exhibit. Page 8, please. In the English, it is page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at item 17, one part of it, the last sentence at page 17, at the very bottom. It reads: "Procedure with prisoners is to be initiated and completed together with the military police organs, engaging commanding officers from the military security and trained organs as necessary." I wanted to ask you the following: You saw the front page. It was a directive issued in 1995. Do you agree that the directive orders that no one should have any contact or be able to treat prisoners of war apart from the military police and competent intelligence organs? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are, and this is what is stated in the directive. That was the standard way of organising of the functioning of any activities pertaining to the prisoners of war. Throughout the war, the military police and military intelligence organs should have been involved in that. No one else. This is merely reaffirming something that had been defined and was supposed to be put in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In other words, the corps were warned yet again that it was the military police that was supposed to be dealing with the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We can put this document away. I wanted to ask you this: Corps -- the various corps received orders from the General Staff to treat prisoners in keeping with the Geneva Conventions; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please show D184 to the witness -- D184A. Your Honours, a clarification for the transcript. Page 53, lines 19 and 20. The witness said that it was the military police and military security who were supposed to work with witnesses. What was put in the transcript was "military intelligence."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, were we discussing military security or military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military security and the military police. I did not mention military security.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore you mentioned the military police and military security.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not mention the military intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Military intelligence service dealt with completely different tasks. It is a separate part, a separate sector within the organ of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that is clear now. Let us have a look at the document. The date of the document is the 27th of July, 1993, sent from the staff of the Main Command to the 3rd Corps command. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a short document. Do you agree that it has to do with the provincial, Mr. Petar Andjelovic, member of the Presidency, concerning certain issues with Croatian citizens? Have a look at the lower portion of the document. Can you see that part, the third paragraph, do you agree that it says the units under your command in this and other similar cases should display discipline and correct behaviour forces which will guarantee security for all the population, regardless of its religious or national affiliation? And do you agree that this document as well is trying to direct the attention of the 3rd Corps to the treatment -- appropriate treatment of prisoners of war according to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this document came into being after the events of Bugojno where there were many victims and casualties on both sides. On one side was the HVO; on the other, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I heard that General Delic was in contact with certain politicians and certain -- with certain clerics. I know when this document was sent out, and it is quite clear in what it states. It directs everyone to behave in keeping with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he merely react to an issue raised by the Provincial Mr. Petar Andjelovic?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a prominent person in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I wish to tender this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if the witness can see document 381.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look and tell me if you agree that this is an order for the implementation of provisions of international humanitarian law from -- dated 8th of May, 1995, addressed to the commands of all corps, among other addressees. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to see the phrase "I order." General, please take a look at that. This is on the following page in the English version, please. I would like to ask you, Witness: Is it correct that this document also instructs the addressees to implement provisions of Geneva Conventions which are provided to the addressees on these pages?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geneva Convention as a document had already been sent to the units, and they had occasion to study it. I remember when we received this document this was initiated -- this initiated and prompted subordinate units to study and be familiar with provisions of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the following page in the Bosnian version. Please, do you agree that there is strict instruction provided in item 3 which says: "Do not accommodate prisoners of war in areas caught up in immediate combat operations"?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it was defined in this text.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are familiar with the existence of such instructions.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then, General, I'd like to ask you in connection with this the following --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have this document admitted into evidence, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 392.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I would like to ask you about this document the following: You said that you were part of a command which planned the Farz operation. You never heard about any other misconduct addressed at prisoners of war. I could conclude from the document that I saw or from the communication you had you did not receive any information about any mistreatment of prisoners of war during that operation or any killing of prisoners of war. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I was present at briefings and reportings that were organised then, I never heard anybody reporting that they had taken prisoners. I do not recall and I think that assistant military security -- assistant commander for military security, I presume he may have briefed the commander at another point in time. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you do not have any information that anything of the sort was briefed.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about this being the topic of briefings. I did not hear myself personally anything. But I know that at a subsequent stage around the 20th and the 30th, that two -- or, rather, four people were captured at Kraljica, and I know that they were forwarded to the Zenica prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness another document, and this -- by this I will conclude my cross. Please retrieve document D382. For the record, this document is a document from the 3rd Corps command dated 15th of September, 1995. And, Your Honours, I noticed that this copy is a poor one in the Bosnian language, so I would like to ask that the witness be given this hard copy, and I would like the witness to pay attention to this document and which section of the document I'm about to tell him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First, Witness, can you confirm that this is a 3rd Corps command document dated 15th of September, 1995. And please take a look at page 3, which is page 4 in the English version. Page 4, Your Honours. Mention is being made in this report of the corps or in this part which regulates the security situation. You've taken a look at this section. Can you confirm or can you agree that this text states that the condition and functioning of the security system is satisfactory? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That the forces conducted a search of the newly liberated territory and that during the course of the day some ten Chetniks were liquidated and that the action is continuing; and that in the newly liberated visits of Vozuca, military police and MUP forces together control the territory, and can you see that on the 15th of September prisoners of war are treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and that they are organisationally being transferred to the CPRVZ. I presume this is a POW reception centre. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that this is how the General Staff received this information. What the acronym CPRVZ stands for is the reception of prisoners of war centre in Zenica. So this centre was not under a tree somewhere in the field, so to speak. Security organs the military police, and once captured, would escort prisoners of war to this military prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this report mentions prisoners of war that are being treated in compliance with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be concluded from this report, and I do believe that this was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the 3rd Corps had no information that prisoners of war are being mistreated or killed on -- by anybody in their zone of responsibility until that date. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such information reaching the command. Had there been, they would have been forwarded to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. But before that, I would like this document to be tendered into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I do have some follow-up questions, Your Honour. I see that we're approaching time designated for the break. I believe these questions might go longer than the five minutes that we might have before that. I leave it to your discretion as to whether we should take the break now or if I should ask a few questions and then we could go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, that's something like seven minutes. I'm sure more than seven questions can be asked. Let's make use of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, you mentioned in your testimony that -- I believe it was page 26, lines 18 through 20 -- you said you delivered the map that we've been discussing today personally to the Commander Delic. Can you tell the Court where that was that you delivered the map and where it was that he signed that map?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must explain and use a couple of minutes for that. I remember to -- that I've carried a complete plan of an operation to the Supreme Command Staff at Kakanj. I'm not sure, but I think that that plan was left there for one night to be studied by the professional and expert services of the General Staff. I cannot remember exactly whether I delivered this plan for the signature of General Delic or my commander, because there was several occasions during the war where plans had to be carried and delivered. Sometimes my commander would do so; sometimes I would. The way that happened in Mostar in the 7th Corps. I'm not sure whether I did it every time, but at least once I did deliver it for it to be studied, but I'm not sure whether I went back to collect it. I'm not sure whether I did go back to collect it. It is possible. It's just that my memory does not serve me well. Maybe I may be reminded of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my own edification, if we can just get a clearer answer: Is it your testimony that you did deliver this map but you didn't fetch it -- you're not sure whether you fetched it, or is your testimony that on one occasion you delivered a map but you didn't fetch it but you can't say which map it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this map, this is the map I'm referring to, the map of the Farz operation. Once I delivered the whole plan, I'm not sure whether it was returned for further elaboration and I'm not sure whether I brought that same plan for signing. If it was not sent back for further elaboration, it was signed, because we saw the map with the signature on it. But what I cannot claim is I'm -- that I'm sure that I brought it or that the commander of the corps brought it there. They are the only two persons who could have done it, me or the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Wood. I give up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when you say, Mr. Jusic, that it was brought "there," where do you mean? Where exactly was this map signed?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Kakanj. To the forward command post at Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As the 3rd Corps chief of staff, did you ever see Rasim Delic in the 3rd Corps command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I assumed my duty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see this question being derived from my cross-examination. I did not dwell on this in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this goes to the part of the cross-examination relating to the alleged lack of communication between different units in the ABiH. I believe this goes to that part of it, in that way is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't you talk about communication rather than talk about seeing him in the 3rd Corps headquarters, 3rd Corps command headquarters. And if he tells you about communication, you can ask him where that communication took place. And if it took place in that, he will tell you. [Microphone not activated] And then at least you are making a basis -- you are laying your foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pardon. I think -- I think try to restrict yourself to communication and if you want to build up to communication in the 3rd Corps, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: On the question of communication, Mr. Jusic, we heard testimony that during the cross-examination that there was difficulties in communication among the different units of the 3rd Corps, among the different units of the ABiH. Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 2561 -- I'm sorry, document P02561, please. And I see, Your Honour, it is fifteen after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it's convenient for you, but if you want to show the document, do say so. What do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It is convenient to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, in that event then we'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Again if document P02561 could be brought up in e-court so that the witness can see that. I see that's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Jusic, could you tell the Court what is this document?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the operational log of the observation post of the commanders. After that, the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what would be the purpose of this document? What would be the purpose of producing this document in terms of military necessity?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a document practically did not have any significance at the moment when it was produced, because this document contained notification of certain information maintained by the duty operational officer in the duty operational centre or a person appointed by the duty operational officer, and the purpose of the information maintained in such a document was as a reminder at a later date or for study purposes of -- if anybody were studying and trying to decide what was going on at that precise moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was it important that the information in this document be accurate?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was important, but it -- this information did not have immediate use, because everybody in the command had these information available. So this log may have an importance for later historical analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If page 2 of that document could be shown to the witness, please. And this would be page 1 of the English translation. If I could draw your attention, sir, to numbers 4 and 5. If you could read those to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the end of the entry for item 5 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, the end for -- the end for number 5 spills on to page 6 of the English translation. There's a few words there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read those, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. We came from point 5. Now we see point 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see that, Your Honour. So it's going to be page -- I might have misspoken. It's page 2 of the English. Item 6 spills on to page 2 of the English. And I see that it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Item 5, yes. Item 5 spells on to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Jusic, can you tell us what is meant by the designation 09.09.95 19.15 on number 4?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the date of the 9th of September, 1995, and the time 19 hours and 15 minutes. This is the moment when this information was jotted down, when this entry was entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could tell us, please, what would be meant by the phrase "all communications operating."

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that wired communication had been checked, those wire communications established with units, and that these were functioning. They are in function --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if I --

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could then draw your attention to number 5, what can we conclude by this phrase: "Luke reported that all units which operate according to plan F are doing all right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours objection, only now did I realise what it was about. When I asked, during my cross, the witness about communications, we very clearly discussed communications, very poor communications during 1992 and 1993, and I did not touch upon communications during the unfolding of the Operation Farz. If you may recall, we discussed the period of 1992 and 1993 and the poor communication and not within this time frame discussed right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this goes to testimony not from earlier today but from yesterday. And as I recall, there was discussion about poor communications throughout the war. I believe that showing this document to the witness would be important to add some context to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that in fact yes, there was this discussion. Do you have any comment to make on that yesterday? Well, in that event, then the question will be allowed and the objection will be overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So again, Mr. Jusic, what can we conclude about communications by the line "Luke reported that all which operated according to plan F are doing all right"?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I'll be able to explain; however, this, what is stated here, means that the positions that were captured by units, which means the observation posts and command posts, and that the new communications were established. This is what is done in such a situation. Field phone lines were being established because of a very small distances, distances of maybe 3 to 4 kilometres. Or in the process of continuing the operations, there would be maybe 10 kilometres of field telephone, and units were equipped by a certain amount of field cables or wires which are on wheels; the length is 750 metres. And they are prepared before combat operations. We're not discussing here communications between commands and units. These communications in question did function, were operational, because the previous night cable had been laid to be used by inductor telephone or field telephone. I believe that such telephones were used in World War I and World War II and now they were used in the third Bosnian war. We're not discussing radio relay communications or permanent communication nodes, but wired communications between combat units during combat operations. These communications had to function because otherwise some officers should have been put in prison for failing to establish such communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention then to item 21. This is on page 4 of the B/C/S version and page 4 of the English. If you could read that to yourself, please, sir, and let us know when you've had to chance to --

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one? Which item, please? Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what, sir, does this indicate about communications between the field and the corps command?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This corroborates what I just said. Those temporary communications were established with the observation post, et cetera, up -- down to the lowest level of units, to companies and even platoons, if the equipment was available. And throughout that system, whoever was -- had access to the network of the PTT -- no, I correct myself, not PTT but wires for field telephones, could phone anybody else if they knew their code name, which was confidential. This is possible, this what has been described, because a commander could have been reached through the switchboard of the brigade and the switchboard of the division and could reach the commander of the 3rd Corps. Of course, this is not a usual method, but there were technical capabilities for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not object to this had the Prosecutor asked these questions during his examination-in-chief, but what I did discuss yesterday and today was the general state of affairs in -- in terms of communication between commands and units and not particular communications during a particular operation. What I did ask the witness about was the relationships in terms of plans between the 3rd Corps and the Supreme Command Staff. I see no reason for reopening this examination. They could have done that during their examination-in-chief, but now they're trying to enter through the back door. Otherwise, I would have done so myself. I did not ask anything pertaining to this issue in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, I'm asking questions about communication because it was raised during the cross-examination. It sounds as if the -- the objection this time is very similar in substance to the objection that was just overruled. The Prosecution submits that the ruling should stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the new dimension that is coming in this objection is that in the cross-examination, the lines of communications that were being discussed were communications between the 3rd Corps and the command -- the command -- control command. Now you are asking about communication on the field. Do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I believe that this does go to the issue of general communication, Your Honour. I believe that when the issue of communication or lack of it was raised, it was among the different units and it was also to the General Staff. I do have some material that will address this latter issue as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to refer us to a page and line shown in the cross-examination where communication on the field was raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I cannot. I don't have that in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you say it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That is my recollection, yes, Your Honour, though I can't cite -- I can't cite to a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us the context in which it was discussed and what was being discussed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's -- it was the discussion about how communication was hindering and even hindering the specific execution of certain operations. I believe the general answered a question that it was actually not just that it was a bad communications but that the communications were so poor that they put certain operations at risk. That's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can cite to something in the record that might assist the Trial Chamber in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what did you say, Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt your conferring there, but I do have a citation. If you go to page 2541, this is from yesterday's transcript. If you look at line 10, the question begins: "Another thing, communication was very poor with subordinated units, in your case in the 3rd Corps. This obtained until the end of the war; is that correct?" Then the answer is: "Yes, that's correct. Communications were through messenger." And that answer goes on through line 17 of page 2541.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: 2541, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Page 2541, yes. And, Your Honour, if I might, then, on to page 18 there's a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Line 18, page 2541.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Essentially, Your Honours, if you focus on lines 10 through the bottom of the page, that, I believe, provides a basis for me to ask these questions now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I had in mind. Yesterday with the witness I discussed the communication between the 3rd Corps and the units in the field in general. Today the Prosecutor is asking -- well, you can see for yourself. And what the witness told me yesterday was that the relay hubs were being -- were destroyed and couriers were being used, and today the Prosecutor is asking about communication inside a specific military operation. That is a very specific pointed question. It has nothing to do with the communication in general that I discussed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, Madam Vidovic, you -- you are trying to explain today what was asked yesterday. That -- that line that we were referred to does talk of communication with subordinates, and, I'm sorry, I'm going to rule you out of order. I'm going to overrule that objection for that reason. So you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention, Mr. Jusic, to item 38, which is page 7 of the English and page 6 of the Bosnian version. And let us know when you've had a chance to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: 38. Yes, sir, 38.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What does this indicate to you, sir, about communication between the 3rd Corps and the -- the General Staff at the time indicated here?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know the way communication functioned. This item tells me that the chief of staff of the General Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina called the commander of the 3rd Corps and asked him about the ongoing combat activities since the commander of the 3rd Corps for various reasons failed to submit his report. To me this means that at the moment when they had that conversation, he managed to establish the connection. It doesn't mean, however, that communication was perfect. There were radio relay links. However, all those devices were prone to becoming inoperative, and they could easily be interfered with or jammed. This tells me that General Hadzihasanovic simply calls the commander of the 3rd Corps and that they discussed the ongoing combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention now to -- finally, this is the last one, item 43, which is on page 8 of the English and on page 7 of the original. And just let us know when you've had a chance to take a look at that entry, General.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, in the English, this reads: "General Staff of the ARBiH submits an interim combat report." Can you explain to us that entry might mean?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the duty operations officer at 10 hours and 18 minutes wrote down the following: That from the command of the 3rd Corps a report was sent to the General Staff, and it was an interim combat report, sent to the General Staff of the ARBiH. In the fourth column, it says it was sent to the operations centre of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers P02561 into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 394.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions now about the map, very briefly. We don't have to get the map out again, but some of the notations might need some context. First of all, the Judges asked some questions about what you referred to as the 7th Chivalrous Liberation Brigade. Do you recall that, sir? I'm sorry, the 7th Muslim Chivalrous Liberation Brigade or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I said on that topic. I said that the acronym on the map specifies what unit was active in that part of the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And this is strictly a notation question. If you could tell the Court, please, what's the relation between that brigade that you mentioned and the brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade, that we've heard testimony about earlier?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not understand. The connection between the 7th Muslim Brigade and ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And the 7th Chivalrous Muslim Liberation Brigade.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same unit. It was termed "chivalrous" by the General Staff. Many units of the 3rd Corps carried titles such as "glorious," and then the next level that would serve to praise a subordinate command would be the "chivalrous". Therefore these two are the same units, and the full name is the 7th Chivalrous Muslim Liberation Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to clear up something else that was in the record. You said on -- I wrote down page 39, lines 10 to 12. I know that that isn't exactly accurate, but it was earlier today. It was page 39 of today's transcript. You said the El Mujahid detachment was not part of the 3rd Corps and then went on to explain that it was part of the 35th Division. Just to clear up any confusion, was the El Mujahid detachment a part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having said that it was not a part of. I don't think such a mistake could have been made by me. Officially, in terms of establishment and by an order of the superior command, one of the units of the 3rd Corps was the El Mujahid detachment since mid-1993. We are not discussing here the issue of command and control and any problems thereof, but at the time of this operation, the command of the 3rd Corps had the legal right to resubordinate the El Mujahid detachment to the 35th Division. In terms of all elements of combat readiness, starting with command and control, down to logistics. Practically speaking, it was not part of the command of the 3rd Corps but of the 35th Division, up until a certain moment when the command of the 3rd Corps, by its order, requests the detachment back as part of its own establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And to whom did the commander of the 35th Division report directly?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 35th Division was directly answerable to the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Finally, one final question: On page 4 from yesterday, lines 8 through 10, you said "Some organs of the General Staff were there," meaning in Kakanj, at the command post. And you listed some of those.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember what I was talking about. Certain command organs of the General Staff were in Zenica for a while. After the January 1994 order, they were stationed in Kakanj. If this refers to Kakanj, then I must have said the organs of the General Staff, and these are the branches department, including the artillery, the armoured units, the communications, the anti-aircraft units, the ABHO, that is, anti-biological chemical warfare unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Vidovic, you started talking while the interpreter was still talking. Can you stand up. What did you want to say, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 75 --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 75, I no longer seem to be able to find the line. The witness was talking about certain organs of the staff of the General Staff, and it keeps repeating -- being repeated organs of the General Staff, but the witness is making a distinction between the organs of the General -- of the staff of the General Staff and organs of the General Staff. Perhaps the witness could clarify it. I found it, Your Honour, page 75, lines 7 and 8. It says: "I have to say that organs of the General Staff and parts of command," and so on and so forth. Can you clarify, Witness? Perhaps the Prosecutor can ask the question. Were you talking about the organs of the staff of the General Staff or about the organs of the General Staff? Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Vidovic, let's just be clear where we are -- what we are talking about. Did you say page 75, lines 7 and 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, just a second. Lines 7 and 8 on my -- on my monitor here doesn't seem to -- to be the same as the other one. It says -- mine says "you said the El Mujahid detachment was not part of the 3rd Corps and then went on to explain that it was part of the 35th Division." That's what my line 75 -- line 7 and 8 of page 75 says. But having said that, I see -- now it's disappearing on the other screen: "And these are the branches department, including the artillery." Now it's gone. On the screen over which I have no control.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it now. I don't know, Your Honours. I no longer have it on the screen. But it was precisely as I described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to go to the screen that you are able to control with your mouse?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 76, line 9: "[In English] I must have said the organs of General Staff." That's where he didn't say "organs of the General Staff" but "organs of the staff of the General Staff." Today, if you remember, during his testimony he made a distinction between this staff and the General Staff; whereas, in the record it says "organs of the General Staff." There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I have nothing further to add to this discussion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me add to the confusion. I also don't understand what is meant by "organs of the General Staff" or "organs of the staff of the General Staff," you know. If it -- if it could be explained what the organs are, what the staff is, what the General Staff is, and what is part of what, I would -- I would appreciate it. I did hear during cross-examination this was being mentioned, and I just thought, Well, they've left me behind, and I don't know what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, if you could please explain to the Court what is meant when you say "the General Staff."

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "the General Staff," I mean the entire superior command, including all of the sectors, departments, and bodies of the superior command. That is the General Staff. That was headed by General Rasim Delic. The General Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just hold on. When you say you mean "the entire superior command," do you -- are you referring to what is called the Presidency? The War Presidency? It's not that? It excludes Alija Izetbegovic. It ends up with the general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know the exact translation. I said "the General Staff." I didn't say "the Supreme Command, the civilian command." The General Staff is the military -- a part of the military structure. The civilian leadership with Alija Izetbegovic and the rest does not fall under that. I am merely talking about the military Supreme Command that was headed, as I said, by General Delic. That command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can tell us who it was composed of, even if it is not the people's names but the offices. Is it -- it's the commander of the army, who's General Delic. And who else? What other commanders come in in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Delic, commander; deputy commander, Stjepan Siber; another deputy commander, Jovan Divjak. Chief of staff of the General Staff, General Hadzihasanovic; assistant commander for finances, Himzo Hodzic; assistant commander for legal affairs, Getz [phoen] -- I don't know what the rest of the name is; assistant commander for intelligence, General Mustafa Hajrulahovic; assistant commander for security, General Jusuf Jasarevic; assistant -- well, those were the assistants to the commander. They are separate. And then, on the other hand, you have the chief of staff, who was General Hadzihasanovic. Within his staff, he had organs or bodies. I'm using the terms that were official in terms of establishment. Organs or bodies of the staff of the General Staff. Branches or organ. And in the Balkan armed forces, such branches are the artillery, armoured units, anti-aircraft defence, ABHO, that is nuclear biological chemical defence, communications. Those are the branches. I don't think I've left anything out. All this was within the staff of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but no matter what the witness says, we have the same interpretation. It is completely wrong. The man is talking about another staff within the General Staff and the record doesn't reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, you see, Madam Vidovic, the problem is some of your interjections are actually tantamount to leading evidence. Now, you raised a problem about confusion about staff. The Chamber has asked a question to the witness to try and explain that. Now you're saying the witness is not explaining it correctly. Do you want to take over and tell us what the composition of the General Staff was? I don't understand this now, because I told you I'm also confused about the staff and I'm -- and the General Staff and all these staffs that are being mentioned here. We're trying to get the witness to tell us. If the witness is not saying it correctly, you will correct it with your witnesses if you don't have an opportunity to cross-examine this witness. But to interject when he is busy answering a question is highly unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. First and foremost, believe me, I am only trying to have the transcript reflect what the witness had said. There is an insistence here on an erroneous interpretation. God forbid that I should try anything. We can have the tape checked here in the courtroom, since I am deeply insulted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is insulting you, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you said I was trying to lead the witness. I have never done that. I'm trying to say that what was said in Bosnian was incorrectly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an insult, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what should I say? To me it is. I never resort to such actions. I never try to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely am trying to have a correct transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime in the past I had asked you to understand that when the Bench is asking questions, you cannot object. If the Bench is asking questions that are wrong, yours is to correct those questions after the Bench has asked its questions. You are doing today exactly the same thing that you have done then, which you promised you'd never repeat the last time I talked to you about it. Do you remember that? And now you are insulted when I'm telling you that you are leading by saying to this witness that he's not saying the correct thing and you're trying to explain what the correct thing is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, believe me, I'm trying to object to the interpretation, not to the witness's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter's interpretation. The interpreter's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. You --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The man is saying one thing and the transcript is saying another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, Madam Vidovic, if the man is saying one thing and the interpretation is different, all you can say is, "Your Honour, it looks like there's been an incorrect interpretation. Could the witness repeat himself," and let the interpreters listen properly, rather than telling us that things are wrong. And what should be coming on. You should know the kind of questions that you must ask to avoid suggesting any answer to the -- to the witness. I'm very sorry, sir. I don't know whether you are able to go back to where we were. If you are able to, please do. My question was simply I'm trying to understand what is the staff -- the various names. If you can tell me what they are, the General Staff and the staff and -- and all those things. And the organs. What is an organ, what is a staff, and what is the General Staff, and what is each composed of. You have told us what the General Staff is composed of. Can you tell us what the staff is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A staff is an expert organ for the planning of combat actions, activities within the General Staff. It is a separate organ, an expert organ. There may be a problem with regard to the terminology. Body or organ, sector, department. In Bosnian terminology, organ is the term of an organisation. As per levels, we have departments, then sector, then organ. And the staff of the General Staff was a separate staff which comprised organs, as we called them. I cannot use another term. And within this staff, we had organs. And it was labeled "operational training organ" or "department," "artillery organ" or"artillery department," "communications organ" or "communications department." In Bosnian language, if you say "communication detachment or department," this may be associated with privates dealing with communication. And this is why we use the term "organ" for communication. I can go into greater detail about the staff of the General Staff, but I -- maybe it would be best if it were drawn in an organisational chart. This would be the best way for me to express this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying the staff within the General Staff would be a subcommittee of members of the General Staff who are assigned a specific task to accomplish? Perhaps because of their expert knowledge in that area? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that same subcommittee, you call it "staff" at some stage, and at some other stage you call it "organ" because it is part of the General Staff? Is that how I understood your last answer? What is then the organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. An organ is a component part of the staff, of that staff, that specific body which does the planning. The organs are component parts of the staff. I'm very sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And by "organ" you refer to individual members of that subcommittee, or does it refer to further smaller committees into that subcommittee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An organ, the term "organ" used to imply the -- let's take an example: Artillery organ. There were three officers within it: The chief. He was the head of artillery. And there were two or three assistants, clerks. Each organ of an -- a branch of the armed forces within the general -- within the staff of the General Staff used to comprise several personnel as per establishment, as per the estimate of the command. Maybe two, three, or four members of personnel. An organ would have -- comprise several members of personnel. It could be a -- an organ with sub-organs, but we didn't use this terminology. We would have head of an artillery organ and then his assistants, which were clerks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jusic. You've done your best. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing further at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'd like to take you back to the much-debated Exhibit 379, I think it was, the chart of the 3rd Corps. If we could have a look at that on the screen for just a second. And the reason I'm taking you back to this chart is that I also have a bit of difficulty to understand just what were the implications of the changes when the new division was -- was incorporated. So let's have a look first at the chart. Can anybody assist us? Yes, I think that was the one. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'd like to see it on the screen. I don't know if that's possible. Madam Usher, can you -- is there any way of making it more clear? Because it's almost illegible on the screen. And if you could pull it out so that we could focus on the right part of the organigramme. That's right. Yes. Now -- and if you could pull it up a bit, because I think I recall that the Mujahedin detachment was somewhere down at the bottom here. Yes. General, this was the organigramme before the new division was incorporated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the organigramme before the detachment was resubordinated to the division, because the division had existed previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Do we see the division anywhere in this chart?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the division in the left-hand corner in the first column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You can move the document so that we can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. This is that division, to which El Mujahid was resubordinated. It was resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And this happened in -- just to be sure about the time, do you recall when this was done?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but after this document was produced. So if we take that this document was produced in January - and I cannot confirm that - that fact occurred -- the fact of resubordination must have taken part in -- taken place in either April or May 1995, after this organigramme had been produced and after this structure had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, what was the purpose of taking Abu Mali's El Mujahid detachment away from the 3rd Corps and putting it under the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place at a time when I personally was more focused on the preparations for the lifting of the Sarajevo siege operation. I was not in the loop. I did not consult with the commander about this resubordination of this detachment. I can share with you my assumption that it was resubordinated at the request of the commander of the 35th Division, because I know that the 35th Division was quite exhausted and the 328th and 329th Brigades were quite exhausted. The personnel was by defence. And I know personally that the commander of the 35th Division wanted to improve the tactical position in -- towards the Vozuca pocket in the area of Podsjelovo. I don't know whether he had maintained any contacts with anybody before. But this was my assumption because I was not in the loop during the resubordination process, but probably in agreement with the commander and the leader of the El Mujahid detachment, they agreed and decided to resubordinate it to the 35th Division. My assumption is that it was done at the initiative of the 35th Division and in -- and in concert with the leader of the El Mujahid detachment, because without such consent on their part, nothing could have been done with that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before the El Mujahid detachment was resubordinated to the 35th Division, was the Mujahedin -- El Mujahid detachment then placed at the same level as other brigades? That's what it looks like here on the chart. So it would have the same hierarchical status as, for instance, the 7th Muslim Brigade and -- and the other brigades that we see here on -- on the chart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in part. The detachment had to be given a certain status, but the detachment and battalion, these are units of the same strength. A battalion is a battalion but brigades are establishment of higher status. There is a step between them. But when a corps commander issues a task, then commanders of detachment of El Mujahedin should have been attending, because they were directly at that time subordinated to the 3rd Corps command. But I can tell you that the 3rd Corps commander never issued a task or a -- to the El Mujahid detachment in the same manner as he did to brigade commanders, because that -- their representative never attended the briefings where tasks were handed down and that unit never reported back -- I don't know how I'll be understood. Maybe I'm taking too long to explain this -- but that detachment, until it was engaged in -- under 35th Division, had never been successful in anything they did. And this is why I wanted to -- protective measures from this court, because of what I said just now, they never had been successful. They were only used under the 35th Division at Podsjelovo and the Vozuca pocket. They managed to achieve certain tasks. Before that they had not done so. They had not reported back. They had not attended briefings and meetings. And commanding that unit meant that you should obey their orders and no commander wanted to deal with them in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, General. You will appreciate that -- that your testimony on exactly this is very crucial to the trial, so I will pursue my questions, my line of questions, a bit further on -- on this because it is still a bit unclear to me how I should understand what you're saying. And so let me just continue with a couple of more questions. I hear you saying that the 35th Division needed some support because they had had difficulties in their earlier combat activities and they were asking for support. In response to that request, the corps commander then offered to have the El Mujahedin detachment resubordinated to the 35th Division. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he offered. I don't know whether he offered or maybe the commander of the 35th Division requested that. I did not attend this discussion. But it's either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In any case, the 35th Division wanted to have some reinforcement, and they got it in the form of having the El Mujahid detachment subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when they were then subordinated to the 35th Division, was it then the commander of the 35th Division who gave orders to the El Mujahid detachment, to Abu Mula and his people -- Abu Mali. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never attended such meetings, but he was in charge of issuing tasks and orders, be it combat, organisational, and others. There was nobody else to give them tasks, because the corps commander no longer issued tasks to them after they were resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Then let's go back to the situation before and after the resubordination to the 35th division. My question is here: Who controlled the activities of the El Mujahid detachment? Who gave them orders? Was that the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take a look before this, in one of my appearances and in an outbreak of emotions, I said that that detachment had not done anything properly, and I said that they would never attend briefings at the 3rd Corps command, and that they would never submit reports. I don't know whether the commander contacted them personally. Ajman would come, but that was way before. He could not receive any tasks. I know that the issue of records on them and issuing them with confirmations was being resolved. But let me answer your question. The commander was -- corps commander was the only person to issue them with orders. I was not present there. What I can tell you, given that they did not achieve anything, no tasks must have been given to them. I don't know. Probably maybe they've received some tasks, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you -- to put my question very frankly, what was the matter with this El Mujahedin -- El Mujahid detachment? And if you wish to go into private session while you give your answer, you can do so. We can go into private session. That means that your testimony will not be made public.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What was wrong with that detachment? Was that the question? In terms of being given orders or being controlled, I fail to grasp the nub of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise. My mistake. The basis of my question was that you said that this detachment had never been able to do anything. You also said in a sentence or two that nobody wanted to give orders to them and -- and I think you said also that they had been unsuccessful in their earlier missions. So I sense that -- that this detachment, the El Mujahid detachment, was not just an ordinary part of the 3rd Corps. It -- it was a special detachment. And I'm trying to find out from you just how was it special? What was the -- didn't they behave well or were they uncontrollable or -- tell us frankly what you remember from that time. And -- and again, if you feel that you are being asked questions that you would prefer to answer in private session, we can do so.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Private session?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If we could then please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, I do have a few more questions to put to you, so I'm sorry to have to ask you to come back tomorrow. I think we are reconvening at 2.15 tomorrow in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned to quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon tomorrow in the same courtroom. Court adjourned.
